lessons.title: Modeling Inflation
objectives: Compute future prices with compound inflation.
Use CPI to measure inflation and adjust prices.
Determine whether a raise kept up with inflation.
lessons.hook: “A movie ticket cost $4.23 in 1990.” What will one cost when you are 50?

notes.body: Inflation = (CPI₂ − CPI₁) ÷ CPI₁; adjusted price = price × CPI₂ ÷ CPI₁.
A raise below inflation reduces purchasing power.

discussion: Who is hurt most by inflation? Who might benefit?
misconceptions: Inflation adds the same dollars each year.
reflection: How would 4% inflation change your future budget?
lessons.extension: Look up current CPI data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

extend: Model a period of high then low inflation.

lessons.realWorld: The BLS publishes CPI monthly; many benefits adjust with it.

lessons.title: How Much Is Enough? Estimating Retirement Savings
objectives: Project a retirement balance with contributions and growth.
Estimate a nest egg with the 4% guideline.
Identify a savings gap and ways to close it.
lessons.hook: “A million dollars is enough to retire.” True? Depends on what?

notes.body: Contribute more, start earlier, work longer, spend less, invest appropriately.

reflection: What retirement lifestyle do you imagine, and what might it cost?
lessons.extension: Use the Decision Lab “Retirement & Inflation Explorer”.
lessons.realWorld: Social Security statements (ssa.gov) estimate benefits from your earnings record.

lessons.title: Comparing Retirement Accounts and Contributions
objectives: Compute employer matches and unclaimed match.
lessons.hook: Free money quiz: Would you turn down $1,500 a year? Many people do.

notes.body: Pay tax now vs. later; compare current and expected future tax rates.
Employer money may require years of service to fully own.

discussion: Why might a teen with a summer job open a Roth IRA?
misconceptions: Count it as part of salary.
reflection: What contribution rate would you choose at your first job?
lessons.extension: Research current IRA contribution limits on irs.gov.

extend: Model Roth vs. traditional with different growth multiples.

lessons.realWorld: Contribution limits are set annually by the IRS.

lessons.title: Purchasing Power and Real Returns
objectives: Convert future dollars to today’s dollars.
lessons.hook: A statement says you will have $2.1 million at 67. Is that a lot?

notes.body: Low-interest cash loses purchasing power over decades.

discussion: Why do statements show future dollars?
reflection: How will you account for inflation in your own goals?
lessons.extension: Compare a savings account rate with current inflation.

extend: Compute the nominal return needed for a 4% real return.
